quote: it seems unlikely that bond prices will remain the same
content: The pundit does not predict a direction. He judges that "bond prices will remain the same" is less likely than usual on the day of a major announcement, which is a claim about variance, and announcements are exactly what raise variance. Kuttner's result is that yields move on the surprise component of an announcement (Kuttner 2001), and scheduled announcements carry some surprise nearly every time, which is why Treasury yields are more volatile on announcement days than on others. The forecasting literature the note cites is about calling up versus down. The pundit moves time from "same" to "up" and "down" together, which is the one call that literature supports.

quote: pairs of numbers, right and left numbers, which you’d call DS for Dexter-Sinister
content: The joke is aimed at numbers that do not behave like a conserved quantity, and the paragraph's own parenthesis, "Though you do have only 100 minutes," is the argument. Action has to divide a fixed budget, so the pundit must choose one allocation. Dempster–Shafer practitioners concede this when they act: Smets's transferable belief model converts belief functions into a single "pignistic" probability at the moment of decision (Smets & Kennes 1994, Artificial Intelligence). Halpern's counterexample to Cox's theorem has been answered with strengthened axioms that restore the result (Van Horn 2003), and de Finetti's Dutch-book argument reaches single additive probabilities without Cox at all. Imprecise probability is a live research programme, but for an agent with 100 minutes to spend it comes down to one number.

quote: your utility function is logarithmic in time spent preparing the excuse
content: The parenthesis is not slipped in. The essay states it as the condition under which the moral holds. And for what the parable is really about, allocating belief rather than minutes, the logarithm is not optional. The logarithmic score is the only proper scoring rule that depends solely on the probability assigned to the outcome that actually occurs (Bernardo 1979). So an agent rewarded only for how much anticipation it placed on what happened is an agent with log utility over its anticipations. Under a linear reward, reporting one's honest beliefs is not optimal, which is why linear utility is the wrong model of anticipation. Linear and threshold utilities give different allocations of minutes, as they should; they give no coherent allocation of belief.

quote: If only there were an art of focusing your uncertainty
content: The Good Judgment Project's one-hour training module taught the art the essay asks for: reason in probabilities, start from base rates, update in small steps, and guard against both over- and underconfidence (Mellers et al. 2014). An hour of it measurably improved accuracy over a year, which is the strongest evidence available that the art exists and can be taught. The essay's rhetorical question sets up the answer the sequence goes on to give. Untrained people who use numbers are overconfident, and that is why the sequence spends the next hundred essays on training.
